overview: Costa Rica’s independence dates to 1821, before the imported map interval. Coffee transport, public institutions and household technologies shaped the republic. Its 1948 to 1949 abolition of a permanent army became a major constitutional transformation, without making the country free of every conflict or inequality.

periods.title: Independence and a changing economy
periods.summary: Coffee commerce and new communications accompanied the development of republican institutions.

periods.title: Army abolition and constitutional change
periods.summary: A symbolic ceremony in 1948 preceded the constitutional prohibition of a permanent army.

periods.title: Continuing republic
periods.summary: Civilian institutions and a changing economy continued under the new constitutional framework.

items.text: From the mid-nineteenth century, ox teams hauled coffee from the Central Valley to Puntarenas. UNESCO describes journeys lasting ten to fifteen days. Moving a crop to a ship required patient work overland before international trade could begin.

Early twentieth-century cart decoration developed recognizable regional designs, followed by flowers, faces and miniature landscapes. Wheels could announce where a driver came from even before a conversation started. The ornate modern cart developed from a more utilitarian vehicle.

A metal ring striking the wheel hub gives each cart a characteristic sound. Craftspeople selected wood with its acoustic qualities in mind. Here the transport had its own soundtrack, long before anyone fitted a radio.

Coffee growers adopted different varieties over time: tall Typica plants were followed by Bourbon and later shorter forms. Villa Sarchí and Villalobos arose through local mutations. Agricultural knowledge involved observing and selecting plants, not simply repeating one unchanged method.

Large banana plantations developed on the Caribbean side under United Fruit. During the 1930s the industry shifted toward the central and southern Pacific coast. A crop’s changing geography affected where work, settlements and transport networks were concentrated.

The National Museum displays coffee and commercial tokens alongside stamps and banknotes depicting prominent buildings. These surviving objects connect buying, wages and public imagery. They are collection evidence about economic life, not excavated remains of an ancient settlement.

Railways, trams, telegraphs and photography appeared during the late nineteenth century. Later, electricity, household appliances and telephones became more widespread. These changes reached society over time; their invention did not mean every household immediately owned them.

sections.title: A military building becomes a museum

items.text: Bellavista Barracks preserves spaces used for ammunition storage, cells, a kitchen, showers and toilets during the 1920s to 1940s. Even a fortified building needed meals, washing and sanitation. The less glamorous rooms help explain how people actually lived within its walls.

Photographs in the museum trace the barracks’ transformation, while towers, corridors, courtyards and stairways retain evidence of its earlier use. The same structure can serve different institutions, so its surviving appearance does not identify one unchanging purpose.

On 1 December 1948, José Figueres struck a section of the Bellavista wall in a symbolic ceremony abolishing the army. The place later became the National Museum. A remembered political gesture is attached to a specific surviving site.

“Se proscribe el Ejército como institución permanente” means “The army is prohibited as a permanent institution.” This Spanish sentence is Article 12 of the 1949 Constitution. It is an attested legal text rather than a slogan reconstructed from memory.

The same constitutional article provides for police and permits military forces in specified defense or continental-agreement circumstances, always subordinate to civilian authority. The distinction matters: banning a permanent army is not the same as abolishing all public security forces.

ending.text: Costa Rica continues as a republic. The 1948 abolition ceremony and 1949 constitutional provision changed its security institutions; they did not end the state. The map’s 1878 start is a coverage boundary, not the date independence or Costa Rican communities began.
